title: The chant
hook: the Church's own music, sung in unison, named for Gregory

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine: Gregory's pun in a market, and the monks he sent who wanted to turn back. Your line was the mission to the english.

No drums. No chords. No beat to tap your foot to. A single line of melody rises, hangs on one syllable for a long, winding moment, and settles again. A handful of voices or a whole choir, all singing the same notes at the same time, so it sounds almost like one person breathing. The words are Latin, often from the psalms or other scripture. It can be heard in monasteries before dawn, in cathedrals on feast days, in a small parish choir on a Sunday. It's called Gregorian chant, and it carries a pope's name.
screen: `NO DRUMS, NO CHORDS.` → `ONE LINE OF MELODY.` → `MANY VOICES, ONE SOUND.`

segments.voice: Gregorian chant is the Church's own sung prayer: the psalms and texts of the Mass and the hours, set to a single melody sung in unison. Start with the name. Tradition links this music to Pope Gregory, the same Gregory we've been with these past days, and medieval pictures sometimes show him with a dove at his ear, as if the Holy Spirit were singing to him. Some readers think the chant as we have it took shape after his time, and that his name was given to honor him. Either way, the name stuck. Next, the shape. In unison means everyone sings the same note at once. Nobody takes the harmony or the solo. Your voice disappears into the others, and the words float on top. Then, why it's built that way. Benedict's Rule tells monks to stand and sing the psalms so that their mind agrees with their voice. Chant is made for that. It goes at the speed of the words, with no beat to march to, so you follow the text and the breath. And Saint Paul tells the early Christians to speak to one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in their hearts to the Lord. Now, the Church today. The Second Vatican Council says the Church recognizes Gregorian chant as especially suited to the Roman liturgy, and that it should have a first place in worship, other things being equal. Here, after a week of monks and a pope, is a way of singing the psalms: one voice made of many.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S SUNG PRAYER.` · `NAMED FOR GREGORY.` · `EVERYONE ON ONE NOTE.` · `MIND IN TUNE WITH VOICE.` · then, large: `ONE VOICE.`

segments.voice: If you can, play some chant and let it run; if not, remember the sound from the start of this lesson, one line rising and falling, many voices on the same note. Either way, don't follow the Latin; follow the breath, and let your breathing slow to the pace of a long syllable. If you pray, let the chant carry your prayer without words.
Gregorian chant. The Church's sung prayer, a single melody sung in unison, named for Pope Gregory. Today's word.
Your line: one voice. Many singers, and no one needs to stand out. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic monasteries and some parishes and cathedrals sing Gregorian chant at Mass and in the Liturgy of the Hours, and the Church's books keep its Latin melodies.

chat.says: Why does Gregorian chant have no harmony and no beat?
options: It's one melody sung in unison, at the speed of the words, so mind and voice agree.
Its harmony and beat were lost over the centuries, and only the bare tune survived.
Pope Gregory banned harmony, saying only one singer should pray aloud at a time.

notes: Sacrosanctum Concilium 116: the Church acknowledges Gregorian chant as specially suited to the Roman liturgy; other things being equal it should be given pride of place. Paraphrased (modern translation not public domain).
Rule 19: 'ut mens nostra concordet voci nostrae'. Paraphrased; confirm.

Attribution to Gregory: framed as 'tradition links'; 'some readers think the chant took shape after his time' reflects the scholarly debate (Frankish/Roman chant). Confirm framing; 'What's certain is that the Church named it for him' should be checked.
Medieval images of a dove at Gregory's ear: from the legend in John the Deacon's life of Gregory. Confirm it's acceptable as an image description.
Hook: 'a dozen voices, or forty, or two' is illustrative, not a statistic; editor may simplify.
